```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(bssd)
```

```{r helpers, include = FALSE}
# results and settings of the installed reproduction and validation scripts
read_results <- function(folder, name) {
  read.csv(system.file(folder, "results", name, package = "bssd",
                       mustWork = TRUE), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
# value assigned at the top level of an installed validation script
script_value <- function(script, name) {
  exprs <- parse(system.file("validation", script, package = "bssd",
                             mustWork = TRUE))
  for (e in exprs) {
    if (is.call(e) && identical(e[[1L]], as.name("<-")) &&
        identical(e[[2L]], as.name(name))) {
      return(eval(e[[3L]], baseenv()))
    }
  }
  stop("'", name, "' is not assigned in ", script, call. = FALSE)
}
fmt <- function(x, digits = 4) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
fmt_e <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 1)
fmt_n <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
# MCMC comparisons of a validation script. The tolerance of each item is four
# Monte Carlo standard errors. For the median, the reference is 0.5 and the
# compared value is the MCMC proportion of draws below the bssd median.
mcmc_table <- function(v, rr = "r") {
  v <- v[v$judgement != "INFO", ]
  stat <- sub("^.*_", "", v$id)
  med <- stat == "MED"
  quantity <- stat
  is_p <- grepl("^P[0-9]", stat)
  quantity[is_p] <- sprintf("P(%s > %s)", rr, sub("^P", "", stat[is_p]))
  quantity[stat == "PROB"] <- sub(" [|] data[)].*$", ")",
                                  v$quantity[stat == "PROB"])
  quantity[med] <- sprintf("P(%s <= bssd median)", rr)
  quantity[stat == "MEAN"] <- sprintf("mean of %s", rr)
  quantity[stat == "IPP"] <- "placebo incidence"
  quantity[stat == "IPD"] <- "study drug incidence"
  bssd_value <- ifelse(med, v$reference, v$bssd)
  mcmc_value <- ifelse(med, v$bssd, v$reference)
  data.frame(data = sub("^[A-Z]+_([A-Z][0-9]+)_.*$", "\\1", v$id),
             quantity = quantity, bssd = bssd_value, mcmc = mcmc_value,
             difference = bssd_value - mcmc_value, se = v$tolerance / 4,
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
show_mcmc <- function(m) {
  knitr::kable(data.frame(Data = m$data, Quantity = m$quantity,
                          bssd = fmt(m$bssd), MCMC = fmt(m$mcmc),
                          Difference = fmt_e(m$difference),
                          SE = fmt_e(m$se),
                          Ratio = fmt(abs(m$difference) / m$se, 2)),
               align = "llrrrrr")
}
# effective sample sizes of the posterior probabilities P(r > c)
ess_range <- function(v) {
  note <- v$note[grepl("_(PROB|P[0-9.]+)$", v$id)]
  range(as.numeric(sub("^.*ESS ([0-9]+).*$", "\\1", note)))
}
# comparison of the default integration grid with a finer grid or with the
# Python reference (validate_convergence.R)
show_convergence <- function(v) {
  parts <- regmatches(v$quantity, regexec(paste0(
    "^(.*), (finer grid vs default|Python reference vs default|",
    "Python reference vs finer grid), (.*)$"), v$quantity))
  parts <- do.call(rbind, parts)
  err <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(sub("^reported error ", "", v$note)))
  knitr::kable(data.frame(Data = parts[, 4], Comparison = parts[, 3],
                          Quantity = sub(" [|] data[)]$", ")", parts[, 2]),
                          Reference = fmt(v$reference, 6),
                          bssd = fmt(v$bssd, 6),
                          Difference = fmt_e(v$abs_diff),
                          `Error estimate` = ifelse(is.na(err), "",
                                                    fmt_e(err)),
                          check.names = FALSE),
               align = "lllrrrr")
}
```

## Model

The exponential Bernoulli (EXP_BERN) model of Duncan (2026, Section 3.3)
assumes constant hazard rates, like BDRIBS, but models whether each subject
had the event during the individual follow-up time instead of the number of
subjects with the event. For subject $i$ with the follow-up time $t_i$, the
event indicator $Y_i$ follows the mixture of two Bernoulli distributions,
$$P(Y_i = 1) = w_p \{1 - \exp(-\lambda_p t_i)\} + w_d \{1 - \exp(-r \lambda_p t_i)\},$$
where $w_p = 1 / (k + 1)$ and $w_d = k / (k + 1)$ are the proportions of
subjects on placebo and on the study drug for the randomization ratio $k:1$,
$\lambda_p$ is the hazard rate on placebo and $r$ is the rate ratio of the
study drug to placebo. The priors are
$$\lambda_p \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\lambda_{HP} PT_{HP} / DF, PT_{HP} / DF), \quad r = \frac{p}{k (1 - p)}, \quad p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b),$$
with the shape and rate parameterization of the Gamma distribution, as in
BDRIBS (`vignette("bdribs1")`). Duncan (2026) uses the Beta(0.5, 0.5) prior
for $p$. A signal is declared when
$P(r > \theta_c \mid \mathrm{data}) > P_{\mathrm{cutoff}}$.

The arguments of `expbern_post()` correspond to the symbols as follows.

| Symbol | Argument | Description |
|---|---|---|
| $Y_i$ | `y` | event indicator of each subject (1 if the subject had the event during follow-up) |
| $t_i$ | `t` | follow-up time of each subject |
| $k$ | `k` | randomization ratio of study drug to placebo |
| $\lambda_{HP}$ | `lambda_hp` | event rate in the historical placebo data |
| $PT_{HP}$ | `pt_hp` | total patient time of the historical placebo data |
| $DF$ | `df` | discount factor |
| $(a, b)$ | `p_prior` | shape parameters of the Beta prior of $p$ (default `r deparse(formals(expbern_post)$p_prior)`) |
| $\theta_c$ | `rr0` | critical value of $r$ (default `r formals(expbern_post)$rr0`) |
| $P_{\mathrm{cutoff}}$ | `cutoff` | posterior probability threshold (default `r formals(expbern_post)$cutoff`) |

`t`, `lambda_hp`, `pt_hp` and the optional time `t_star` for the cumulative
incidences must be in the same time unit. Because the likelihood stays
positive as $r \to \infty$, the posterior mean of $r$ is infinite when the
second shape parameter of the Beta prior is 1 or less, as for the default
prior; the posterior median is then the summary of $r$ to use.

## Example

The following data are simulated with `sim_blinded()`: 300 subjects
randomized 1:1 with uniform entry over 26 weeks, 52 weeks of planned
follow-up, and exponential times to the event with cumulative incidences of
10% on placebo and 20% on the study drug at week 52. At the blinded analysis
at week 52, the follow-up times are between 26 and 52 weeks.

```{r data}
set.seed(2026)
rate_of <- function(ip, t) -log(1 - ip) / t
d <- sim_blinded(n = 300, k = 1, accrual = 26, follow_up = 52,
                 analysis_time = 52, dist = "exponential",
                 par_p = rate_of(0.10, 52), par_d = rate_of(0.20, 52))
head(d[, c("id", "follow_up", "event")])
```

The prior of $\lambda_p$ is based on a historical placebo group of 150
subjects followed for 52 weeks with the incidence of 10%, discounted by
$DF = 2$.

```{r fit}
fit <- expbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1,
                    lambda_hp = rate_of(0.10, 52), pt_hp = 150 * 52,
                    df = 2, t_star = 52)
fit
summary(fit)
```

The posterior probabilities for other critical values of $r$ are obtained
with `rr0`; `details = FALSE` skips the quantiles of $r$:

```{r rr0}
vapply(c(1, 1.5, 2), function(q) {
  expbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1,
               lambda_hp = rate_of(0.10, 52), pt_hp = 150 * 52, df = 2,
               rr0 = q, details = FALSE)$prob
}, numeric(1))
```

## Numerical integration

`expbern_post()` integrates the two-dimensional posterior numerically on the
coordinates $\log \lambda_p$ and the prior distribution function of $p$. A
coarse grid locates the region that holds almost all posterior mass;
Gauss-Legendre quadrature is used for $\log \lambda_p$ and Chebyshev
interpolation for the second coordinate (see `?expbern_post`). With
`control$check = TRUE`, the default, the computation is repeated on a finer
grid, the finer result is returned, and the absolute difference in `prob` is
reported as the error estimate (`fit$integration$error`, here
`r fmt_e(fit$integration$error)`).

```{r convergence-data, include = FALSE}
conv <- read_results("validation", "validate_convergence.csv")
conv <- conv[grepl("^C_E", conv$id), ]
```

The script `inst/validation/validate_convergence.R` compares the default
grid with a much finer grid for the following data sets. The column Error
estimate is the error estimate reported with the default grid.

```{r convergence-table, echo = FALSE}
show_convergence(conv)
```

The largest difference is `r fmt_e(max(conv$abs_diff))`, and all
`r nrow(conv)` items are `r paste(unique(conv$judgement), collapse = ", ")`.

## Comparison with MCMC

```{r mcmc-data, include = FALSE}
jags <- read_results("validation", "validate_jags.csv")
v <- jags[grepl("^J_E", jags$id), ]
m <- mcmc_table(v)
exp_cases <- script_value("validate_jags.R", "exp_cases")
n_burn <- script_value("validate_jags.R", "n_burn")
n_iter <- script_value("validate_jags.R", "n_iter")
n_chain <- script_value("validate_jags.R", "n_chain")
model_exp <- script_value("validate_jags.R", "model_exp")
ess <- ess_range(v)
is_prob <- grepl("^P[(]", m$quantity)
pick <- function(name) vapply(exp_cases, function(cs) cs[[name]], numeric(1))
ids <- vapply(exp_cases, function(cs) cs$id, character(1))
prob_rows <- v[grepl("_PROB$", v$id), ]
events <- sub("^.*events = ([0-9]+).*$", "\\1", prob_rows$quantity)
names(events) <- sub("^J_(E[0-9]+)_PROB$", "\\1", prob_rows$id)
```

The script `inst/validation/validate_jags.R` compares `expbern_post()` with
MCMC in JAGS for the simulated data sets below. The JAGS model is written
directly from the model specification of Duncan (2026, Section 3.3) and
shares no code with bssd:

```{r jags-model, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
cat(trimws(model_exp), "\n")
```

The results in this section are read from the output of that script
(`validate_jags.csv` in the folder `validation/results` of the installed
package); JAGS is not run when this article is built.

```{r mcmc-settings, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Data = ids, N = pick("n"), k = pick("k"), Events = unname(events[ids]),
  `Placebo (week 52)` = sprintf("%g%%", 100 * pick("ip_p")),
  `Study drug (week 52)` = sprintf("%g%%", 100 * pick("ip_d")),
  `Analysis (week)` = pick("tau"),
  `Prior incidence (week 52)` = sprintf("%g%%", 100 * pick("ip_prior")),
  `Prior of p` = sprintf("Beta(%g, %g)", pick("a"), pick("b")),
  rr0 = pick("rr0"), check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
```

Placebo and Study drug are the incidences used to simulate the data with
`sim_blinded()`, and Prior incidence is the incidence from which `lambda_hp`
is computed; the script gives the other settings. JAGS was run with
`r n_chain` chains, `r fmt_n(n_burn)` burn-in iterations and
`r fmt_n(n_iter)` iterations per chain. The Monte Carlo standard error (SE)
of each MCMC estimate uses the effective sample size of the draws
(`coda::effectiveSize()`); for the posterior probabilities, the effective
sample sizes are between `r fmt_n(ess[1])` and `r fmt_n(ess[2])`. For the
median, the table shows the MCMC proportion of draws below the posterior
median computed by bssd, which should be 0.5. The incidences are the
posterior means of the cumulative incidences at week 52. The column Ratio is
the absolute difference divided by the SE.

```{r mcmc-table, echo = FALSE}
show_mcmc(m)
```

In all `r nrow(m)` items, the bssd value is within
`r fmt(max(abs(m$difference) / m$se), 1)` standard errors of the MCMC value,
and `r sum(abs(m$difference) / m$se <= 2)` items are within two standard
errors. The largest absolute difference in a posterior probability is
`r fmt(max(abs(m$difference[is_prob])))`, while the SEs of the MCMC
probabilities are between `r fmt(min(m$se[is_prob]))` and
`r fmt(max(m$se[is_prob]))`. Differences of this size are expected from the
Monte Carlo error of MCMC alone, so the difference between the numerical
integration of bssd and MCMC is negligible in practice. The validation script
judges an item PASS when the difference is at most four standard errors;
`r sum(v$judgement == "PASS")` of the `r nrow(v)` items are PASS.

## References

Duncan, B. (2026). Robust safety monitoring and signal detection using
alternatives to the standard Poisson distribution. *Journal of
Biopharmaceutical Statistics*, 36(2), 227-244.
<https://doi.org/10.1080/10543406.2024.2395532>
